blocks.text: **The problem.** Implement a first-in-first-out **queue** using only **two stacks**. Your class `MyQueue` must support `push(x)` (add x at the back), `pop()` (remove and return the front item), `peek()` (return the front item) and `empty()`. You may only use standard stack operations: push to the top, look at or pop the top, size and is-empty. `pop` and `peek` are only called when the queue isn't empty.

blocks.alt: A stack holding 1, 2, 3 with 3, the newest, on top. Pouring it into a second stack — popping each item and pushing it onto the other — reverses the order, so 1, the oldest, ends up on top, ready to leave first.

blocks.text: Example

blocks.code: push(1)   push(2)   peek() -> 1   pop() -> 1   empty() -> false

blocks.text: A stack hands back its **newest** item; a queue must hand back its **oldest**. The one tool we have is in the picture above: pouring a stack into another **reverses** it, which brings the oldest item to the top.
In JavaScript a plain array is a perfect stack — `push` and `pop` both work at the end in O(1) — so there's no hidden cost here.
1. Brute force: keep the oldest on top, at every push

Keep stack `s1` arranged with the **oldest item on top**, so `pop` and `peek` work straight away. The price is paid by `push`: the new item must go to the **bottom**. Pour all of `s1` into `s2`, push `x` onto the now empty `s1`, then pour everything back on top of it.

blocks.alt: Pushing 4 when s1 holds 3, 2, 1 with 1, the oldest, on top. Step 1: pour s1 into s2, which now holds 1, 2, 3 with 3 on top. Step 2: push 4 onto the empty s1. Step 3: pour s2 back onto s1, which now holds 4, 3, 2, 1 with 1 still on top. Every push moves every item twice.

elements.text: 4 is at the bottom, 1 (the oldest) is still on top: every push moves every item twice
elements.originalText: 4 is at the bottom, 1 (the oldest) is still on top: every push moves every item twice

blocks.text: **push O(n) — 2n moves; pop, peek and empty O(1); space O(n).** (In Java, `ArrayDeque`'s `push`, `pop` and `peek` work at one end, so it's the recommended stack — the old `Stack` class is slower.)
2. Optimal: pour only when you have to
The brute force pours everything back after every push — wasted work, because the next push pours it all out again. Instead, give each stack one job and **never pour back**:

items: **outbox** — every `pop` and `peek` comes from here. Its top is the oldest item.

blocks.text: When the outbox runs **empty** and someone wants the front, pour the **whole** inbox into it. That flips the order, so the oldest item lands on top. Until the outbox is empty again, there's no reason to touch the inbox: everything in the outbox is **older** than everything in the inbox, so the front of the queue is always on the outbox.

blocks.alt: The inbox holds 4 and 5, with 5 on top; new pushes land here. The outbox holds 3 and 2, with 2 on top; pops and peeks take from here. Every item in the outbox is older than every item in the inbox. The inbox is poured over only when the outbox is empty.

blocks.text: Why is this O(1)? Amortized analysis

A single `pop` can be slow: if the outbox is empty and the inbox holds n items, it pours all n. So the **worst case** for one call is O(n). But follow one **item** through its whole life instead of one call:

blocks.alt: The life of one item, in four stack moves: 1, pushed onto the inbox; 2, popped off the inbox; 3, pushed onto the outbox; 4, popped off the outbox. Steps 2 and 3 happen during one pour. No item is ever poured back, so each item costs at most 4 moves in total.

elements.text: never poured back: at most 4 moves per item, in its whole life
elements.originalText: never poured back: at most 4 moves per item, in its whole life

blocks.text: Every item is moved **at most 4 times**, ever. So any sequence of n operations does at most about 4n stack moves in total — **O(1) per operation on average**. That's what **amortized O(1)** means: some calls are expensive, but they're paid for by all the cheap ones. (Compare the brute force: every push moves every item, so n pushes cost O(n²).)
**push O(1); pop and peek O(1) amortized, O(n) worst case for one call; space O(n).**
3. Best solution: peek without pouring

One small improvement: `peek` doesn't need to pour at all. If the outbox has items, its top is the front. If it's empty, the front is the **oldest item in the inbox** — the one at its bottom — and we can simply remember it: it's whichever item was pushed while the inbox was empty. Now `peek` is O(1) even in the worst case, and only `pop` ever pours.
**push, peek and empty O(1) worst case; pop O(1) amortized; space O(n).** This is LeetCode's official best answer for **Implement Queue using Stacks** (232).
Comparing the three approaches

blocks.alt: Brute force: push O(n) time, O(n) space. Optimal: O(1) amortized time, O(n) space. Best: O(1) amortized, peek O(1) time, O(n) space.

blocks.text: Edge cases to test

items: **Push after a pour** — `push 1, push 2, pop, push 3, pop, pop` must give 1, 2, 3. The new item waits in the inbox behind the outbox's older items.
**peek when the outbox is empty** — `push 5, push 6, peek` must give 5, the oldest, not 6.
**empty()** — true only when **both** stacks are empty; checking just one is a common bug.
**Long runs of pushes, then of pops** — one big pour, then every pop is O(1).

blocks.text: Variations

items: **Queue using one stack** — recursion: pop items off until the bottom one (the oldest) is reached, then push the rest back as the calls return. The call stack plays the second stack, so it's O(n) per pop.
**Min queue** — build the queue from two **min stacks** (stacks that know their minimum); the queue's minimum is the smaller of the two. This gives the sliding window minimum in O(1) amortized.
**Stack using queues** — the mirror problems earlier in this course. There's no amortized trick there: rotating a queue doesn't reverse it.
**Worst-case O(1) queue from stacks** — possible, by pouring a little at a time in the background (a "real-time queue"), but far beyond what interviews ask.
